title: Why the marginal likelihood is hard
blurb: Partially observed data, mixtures of infinitely many Gaussians, naive Monte Carlo

hook.title: Counting every possible completion
hook.text: Half of a photo is torn off. What's the probability of seeing the intact half? You'd have to consider **every possible way the missing half could look**, weigh each by its plausibility, and add them all up. With 30 hidden binary features that's over a billion completions per training photo, per gradient step. Guessing completions at random is hopeless too: nearly all random completions look like static, with probability near zero, so you'd practically never hit the plausible ones.
hook.recall: Remember the torn photo: the marginal likelihood sums over *all* completions of the hidden part, which explodes in number, and random guessing almost never lands on a plausible one. We need a smart proposal $q(z)$.

explore.intro: Two tabs: counting terms, and why uniform/prior-sampling Monte Carlo gives wild estimates.
tasks: Count tab: set 30 features. How long at a billion terms per second?
MC tab: make the likelihood narrow (small $\sigma_x$). Compare the min–max spread of the two estimators.
explore.takeaway: $p(x;\theta)=\sum_zp(x,z;\theta)$ has $2^{30}$ terms for 30 binary latents; naive Monte Carlo fails because most $z$ have tiny $p(x,z)$. Sampling $z$ cleverly (from $q$) tames the variance.

build.template: $\log p(x;\theta)=\log$ {0} $p(x,z;\theta)$; with 30 binary latent features the sum has {1} terms.
build.explanation: Slide 46: “Suppose we have 30 binary latent features, $z\in\{0,1\}^{30}$. Evaluating $\sum_zp(x,z;\theta)$ involves a sum with $2^{30}$ terms.”

questions.prompt: The VAE’s generative model is described as:
options: A mixture of an infinite number of Gaussians
questions.explanation: $z\sim\mathcal N(0,I)$, $p(x|z)=\mathcal N(\mu_\theta(z),\Sigma_\theta(z))$: one Gaussian for each possible $z$.

questions.prompt: In partially observed data, which variables are never observed?
questions.explanation: The torn-off half (latents) is never seen.

questions.prompt: Which statement about naive Monte Carlo for $p_\theta(x)$ is FALSE?
options: We would rarely hit the likely completions by uniform sampling
We need a clever way to select $z^{(j)}$ to reduce variance
It works well in practice for high-dimensional $z$
questions.explanation: “Works in theory but not in practice.”

questions.prompt: What is the “no free lunch” of latent variable models compared with autoregressive ones?
options: They are much more difficult to learn because $p(x)$ is hard to evaluate and optimise
questions.explanation: Slide 44: much more difficult to learn than fully observed autoregressive models.

questions.prompt: *“I estimate $\log p(x)$ by $\log\frac{p(x,z^{(1)})}{q(z^{(1)})}$ with one sample; this is unbiased since $\mathbb E[\log\cdot]=\log\mathbb E[\cdot]$.”* What’s wrong?
options: $\mathbb E[\log\hat p]\neq\log\mathbb E[\hat p]$ (Jensen): the log of an unbiased estimate of $p(x)$ is a biased (downward) estimate of $\log p(x)$
questions.explanation: Slide 68 (optional) points out exactly this inequality.
